title: Institution of the Lord's Supper
aliases: what happened in institution of the lords supper
tell me about institution of the lords supper
why is institution of the lords supper important
summary: Matthew, Mark, and Luke describe Jesus sharing bread and a cup with his disciples during the meal before his arrest. He interprets them in relation to his coming death and to covenant, while Luke also records the instruction to repeat the meal in remembrance. John tells the same final-meal setting differently: it highlights Jesus washing the disciples' feet and his farewell teaching, but does not include the Synoptic words over bread and cup. Reading the accounts together makes both their shared setting and their distinct emphases visible.
historical_context: Matthew, Mark, and Luke place the meal on the night before Jesus' arrest and identify it with Passover. Their accounts describe a shared table, bread, and a cup, but they do not give identical wording or sequence. John also locates Jesus with his disciples at a final meal before the arrest, while emphasizing footwashing and farewell teaching. The Gospel accounts do not specify the meal's precise location or give a detailed menu.
literary_context: The Synoptic accounts place Jesus' interpretation of bread and cup within the final meal and immediately before the events of his arrest and death. Matthew and Mark emphasize the cup as blood of the covenant; Luke also frames the meal as remembrance and places it alongside a dispute about greatness and Jesus' teaching on service. John develops the meal through the washing of feet and the farewell discourse rather than repeating the bread-and-cup scene. The differences help readers attend to what each Gospel chooses to emphasize on Jesus' final night.
covenantal_significance: In Matthew and Mark, Jesus identifies the cup with his covenant blood; Matthew adds that it is poured out for forgiveness. Luke connects the cup with a new covenant and the meal with remembrance. The Gospels therefore present the meal as a way of interpreting Jesus' approaching death, not simply as a final supper. John does not give the same words over bread and cup, but its account places the meal within Jesus' acts and teaching about humble service to his followers.
canonical_role: The Synoptic meal accounts have shaped Christian practice of the Lord's Supper, while John's distinct account keeps service and mutual love in view as part of Jesus' final meal with his disciples. These accounts are related but not interchangeable: three narrate the bread-and-cup words, and John gives a different set of actions and teachings. Their contrast is useful for understanding how the Gospels remember and interpret Jesus' final night.

interpretive_notes.note: Gospel events are both historical and theological centers.
The evangelists present them to shape faith and understanding.
